utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody and to you, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, The Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. General Miletic like yesterday is not present today. A waiver has been received. Prosecution team is Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Vanderpuye from what I can see behind the column, and Defence teams I think it's -- I just saw Mr. Haynes. Where is he? Oh, I see. Yeah, and then I didn't see him anymore. So it's only Mr. Bourgon who is absent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I had to move because the monitor over there wasn't working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But we have these two columns that, at least as far as I'm concerned, are of obstruction. Witness is present. Mr. Trifkovic. Good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are most welcome. You are about to start giving evidence as a Defence witness for the Beara Defence team. Before you do so, our rules require that you make a solemn declaration, which is going to be handed to you, and this is an undertaking to testify the truth. Please read it out aloud.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. Do I take it that you are going to testify in English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. You are free to testify in any other language which is translatable here should you feel so. Mr. Ostojic is going first. You will be with us today and tomorrow for sure. He didn't like it. Okay. So you can cut down your direct, Mr. Vanderpuye will take my advice to do likewise, and we can send him home today.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Mr. President, Your Honours. I'll try to do my best. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, as you know my name is John Ostojic, and I'm one of the attorneys here for Mr. Ljubisa Beara. Can you please state your name for the record?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. My same Srdja Trifkovic. I'm also known to my English-speaking friends as Serg.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trifkovic, we both speak the same language, and sometimes we can overlap as both the person who is asking the questions and the person who is providing the answers. We're going to try to take it slow today even though we will make every effort to conclude with your testimony today. Can you share with us briefly, where do you currently reside?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: I currently reside in Highland Park, which is a north-shore suburb of Chicago, Illinois.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little about your education? What's the highest level of education that you've attained?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: A PhD in European history at the university of Southampton in the UK obtained in the summer of 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you -- presently, do you -- are you employed anywhere?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, as foreign affairs editor of the monthly magazine "Chronicles Published By The Rockford Institute" in the city of Rockford in Illinois.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How long have you held that position?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: For the past nine years.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And prior to that, have you been gainfully employed?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Between 1996 and 1999, I was in academia, first at the University of St. Thomas in Houston, Texas, as a visiting professor for one year; and at then at Rose Hill College in Aiken, South Carolina.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Can you share with us what you did in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: In the first half of 1992, I was completing my one year of post-doctoral research at Stanford -- at the Hoover Institution at Stanford University on a Title 8 grant from the department of state on US policy in the Balkans during World War II. The second half of that year I spent as Chief of Staff of his Royal Highness Crown Prince Alexander Karadjordjevic based in London, England.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And as his Chief of Staff, just briefly describe what your duties and responsibilities were at that time.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: That was a period when the monarchist sentiment in Serbia was on the rise and when believing that the Crown could electrify a position to Milosevic, a sentiment I wholeheartedly shared. I was keen to help him assert himself as a possible factor who could meaningfully contribute to the process of political change in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Trifkovic, you and I know each other, and we've known each other for quite some time, correct?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Longer than I care to remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Can you tell me, also, have you testified before the Tribunal in other cases or in any other case?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: I was an expert witness in March of 2003 in the Stakic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And what expertise did you provide for the Stakic case at that time?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: I provided a background of the Bosnian war in general and the situation in the municipality of Prijedor in particular based not so much on my personal observation of the circumstances but rather on the access to secondary sources, materials, and statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And you recognise, sir, although you were an expert witness in that case that you're being called here in this case as a fact witness?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please pause between questions and answers for the sake of the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Both of you? Yes, please. If you could comply, we'll appreciate that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, following your employment with Crown Prince Alexander in the capacity as Chief of Staff, what, if anything, did you do in terms of employment?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: In the summer of 1993, it became obvious that contrary to my hopes and expectations the crown prince was not going to move to Serbia on a permanent basis, which I believe he should have done especially in view of the ongoing conflicts in the former Yugoslavia, and I was not willing to simply continue as basically a glorified administrator preparing press releases and statements out of the London office, which I believed to be somewhat meaningless. So relying on my previous connections as correspondent for US News and World Report in Belgrade and on my access that I had during the period of my work for him, I decided to work as a freelance journalist, and I had a contract with the Belgrade magazine called Duga, Rainbow, and they also had regular slots in a number of English-speaking publications including at that time also the leading bilingual newspaper of the Serbian community in the United States, Sloboda, Liberty. And I was also providing regular interviews to the electronic media in the UK having spent six years as a radio journalist with the BBC world service in the 1980s. I had connections there, too, and I was regularly interviewed especially when it came to presenting a Serbian point of view in the ongoing conflicts in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Share with us, if you will, if you ever had an opportunity to go to Pale and meet with Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The first such occasion was in my capacity as Crown Prince Alexander's advisor, which was at the end of July of 1993 at the time of the Igman and Bjelasnica operation, when I also brought in my car, a consignment of humanitarian assistance and medicines sent by the crown prince's wife Princess Catherine, and I also had a meeting at that time with a number of political and military leaders in a purely ceremonial capacity conveying the best wishes from the crown prince and delivering the packages to the hospital, Koran [phoen] hospital at Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Were you ever asked to assist with any of the mainstream media from Dr. Karadzic or people from Republika Srpska in connection with -- or based upon your experience as a journalist and being knowledgeable in the Balkan area?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: That initiative came later on. In September of 1993, my wife and I were touring northern France, and we stopped in Geneva where at that time one of the negotiating sessions was going on, and I was personally acquainted with the late professor Nikola Koljevic somewhat more closely than with the others from the Republika Srpska leadership. And it was from him that the initiative came that I would be useful as a spokesperson in some capacity because I think he had seen some of my articles and my media appearances up to that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And did you accept to attain such a position as a spokesman?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the situation was somewhat delicate because accepting the position of an official spokesman would have severely curtailed my capacity to function as a freelance journalist and also to provide the kind of analysis of the political background to the conflict in former Yugoslavia that I wanted to continue doing as I deemed fit. I therefore indicated to Professor Koljevic before he formalized the proposal to Dr. Karadzic that I would accept an informal arrangement in which my ability to continue with my other professional pursuits would not be hindered, and which would also enable me to present and articulate positions and analysis in accordance with my own understanding rather than in accordance with anyone's formal instructions. I also believed that in this way I could provide a more comprehensive and more useful information to the media consumers in the English-speaking world, especially since, to be perfectly frank with you, I was also skeptical about the ability of people in Pale, the ability of people in the Serbian lands in general, to present and articulate their positions in a way that would be both readily understood by the western media consumer and that would be presented in a convincing and coherent manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trifkovic, what was your title, then, if any, at that time?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: My title was the Balkan affairs analyst with close links to the Bosnian Serbs. I was occasionally in the media presentation, actually referred to as the representative or spokesman for the Bosnian Serbs, which I always insisted on correcting because I did not want this impression of a formal relationship to be created, not only because of the fact that I wasn't receiving either instructions or payment from Pale but also because I wanted to give them the ability to obtain plausible deniability of my statements if they happened to be displeased with them so that at all times I could both retain the status of an independent analyst, and the leadership of the Republika Srpska could retain its ability to distance themselves from my analysis as presented to the media, which, by the way, did not happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And we've seen -- or received from the Prosecution some media CDs of you giving speeches to news outlets, and they referred to you as "the unofficial Bosnian Serb spokesman." Would that be a fair way to say it?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: No, because spokesman or spokesperson, again, whether official or unofficial is the person who conveys clearly articulated formal statements or positions of a given entity, which I was very careful to emphasize that I was not in the position to do. But on the other hand, journalists are in the habit of simplifying issues, and if the editor says, give me the Bosnian Serb point of view, they will probably, you know, fill the slot any which way they can even if such a designation which corresponds to the needs of the editorial cycles may fit in neatly with their requirements would not be accurate when it came to my actual role.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. So let me stick, then, with the title that you provided us, and that is as "the Balkan affairs analyst with close links to the Bosnian Serbs." Did you hold that position for any length of time?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: I did until, I believe, first week of September of 1995 when the political leadership of the Republika Srpska decided to authorize Slobodan Milosevic to negotiate on their behalf. I could not possibly continue as someone presented as a person with close links or any links with a political entity that was now hardly more than an offshoot of the Milosevic Pale centre. In fact, I remember saying at one point that -- asking Milosevic to negotiate on behalf of the Republika Srpska was tantamount to entrusting Count Dracula with a blood bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Trifkovic, if you could just give us an idea, and since you started in approximately mid-to late September in the role as Balkan affairs analyst with close links to the Bosnian Serbs, can you tell us in that year how often you would meet with the Republika Srpska leadership just so we can get a general sense of it?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: I spent a week in late November of 1993 in Geneva at the Palestine Nations where I tried to set up some kind of media management for -- I obviously wasn't going to stay there, but I wanted to help them out with the art of composing press releases and formal statements and not relying on improvisation as they had been doing until that time. I am afraid that I was successful in this endeavour to a very limited extent. And after that, during 1994 I paid a total of four visits to the Republika Srpska at times they coincided with my coming to Belgrade on private business or vacations. One or two occasions in 1994 and one occasion in 1995 were purpose-made trips because I simply wanted to find out what was the view from Pale, so to say, at particularly sensitive moments of the Bosnian crisis, such as the Gorazde crisis in 1994, the aftermath of Ex-President Carter's visit in 1995, and ironically in the summer of 1995 I visited Pale because I had already intended to be in Belgrade as part of my summer break without ever suspecting that those days in the month of July would subsequently prove to be critical in many ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And we'll come back to July 1995 a little later in your examination, but just give us an idea. In 1995 other than July, were you at Pale?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: I was at Pale in late January of 1995. I remember leaving Belgrade on Saint Sava's day that year, and I remember it vividly because --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just tell us what day.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: It was 27th of January. I was at Pale 28th and 9th, and I drove back the following day, so probably on the 30th. And in March, I was there just for one day, in March -- I don't remember the exact day. Probably 22nd or 23rd or 24th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And help me with this: After your visit in Pale in July of 1995, did you ever go back to Pale?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Where were you stationed during the time that you were the Balkan affairs analyst?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: I was dividing time between London and the United States. I was at that time still pursuing research subsequent upon my post-doctoral work at Stanford, and I was actually looking for employment in the United States because having been frankly disillusioned with the way that the Republika Srpska leadership, one might say, folded up by entrusting Milosevic with the end game, I prepared the ground in the US for my subsequent move to Houston in the summer of 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar, as I'm sure you are being a historian, with events that were generally considered the September 1993 action?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: I am familiar in the capacity of, you know, someone who takes a great deal of interest in these affairs, but I'm not familiar with them on a firsthand basis. In other words, I have not discussed them with any of the key participants or key players, and I certainly have not been privy to any privileged information concerning their background.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, just give us an idea of what it is from the information that you have.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: The Latin tensions between the political leadership of the Republika Srpska and the military leadership had always been present to some extent. The military leadership was composed to a large extent of the former YPA officers who were viewed by the political leaders belonging to the Serbian democratic party as people with a great deal of ideological baggage in their tow. But my first awareness of these tensions came, actually, during the very first visit to Pale during the and Igman and Bjelasnica operation when I gathered from conversations with other people such as one of the advisors to Dr. Karadzic, that he viewed Karadzic, that operation as detrimental to what he believed was a possible diplomatic political break-through and that he believed that by acting without the clear approval from the civilian leadership, the military was somehow undermining the political and diplomatic efforts of the civilian leadership. I, frankly, did not believe that this was substantively the case, even if Dr. Karadzic believed it to be so. In fact, I was pretty certain that no immediate political diplomatic break-through was on the horizon, and as we had seen subsequent to the summer of 1993, in the fall of 1993, the negotiations in Geneva under Stoltenberg and Owen, which had a promising framework of the three entities that had the attributes of sovereignty, collapsed, torpedoed by the United States just as the previous Owen-Stoltenberg plan had been torpedoed in the spring of '93. The second crisis, if you will, in the relations occurred in September of 1993 with a protest by the war veterans, handicapped and wounded soldiers, and the families of the fallen, and there were two versions of what was going on. One was that of the political leadership, which claimed that this was engineered by the military top brass as a means of putting pressure on politicians and as a means of pointing out the existence of Banja Luka as the alternative power centre to Pale; while on the other hand, the view of the soldiers was that the Serbian democratic party establishment, allegedly both corrupt and inept, was manipulating the perfectly justified grievances of the veterans, the wounded, the handicapped, and the widows and orphans, in order to engineer a show-down with the military that would give them an excuse to replace the top brass of the BSA. And either way, I frankly do not have the information that would enable me even at this stage to pass the verdict, whether it was one or the other or the mix of the two. But either way, it certainly proved that not -- that something was rotten in not the kingdom of Denmark but the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just follow up if you don't mind and clarify. You said BSA. Just tell us what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: I mean VRS, Vojska Republika Srpska or Bosnian Serb Army is the usually shorthand used in...

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. And then you also use the acronym YPA?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: The Yugoslav People's Army or JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I just want to clarify that. Now, when, if at all, was the first time that you heard the name of Ljubisa Beara?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: The first time I heard the name of Ljubisa Beara was during the week I spent in Geneva in late November of 1993, when during the long and arduous negotiating sessions of which I was not -- to which I wasn't privy and obviously was not invited, I spent a few hours in all with the members of the Republika Srpska delegations security detail. Being both a journalist and a historian, I was very interested in the views and experiences of these young men who were all veterans of the early battles in the summer of 1992 and who being, you know, mostly simple folk from the grass roots of the Bosnian/Serb public at large were providing -- I don't want to sound condescending about this, but it was the genuine vox populi. It was something that one doesn't get in a raw form unless you actually spend a long time in the Republika Srpska, which I wasn't able to do. And so just listening to them chatting among themselves, joking, reminiscing, and commenting provided me with a fascinating insight into the -- you know, the nitty-gritty of the perception of events on the ground. And it was in this context that I heard them refer to Ljubisa Beara's appointment as "bezbednjak," chief of security of the Bosnian/Serb army, with displeasure and even indignation because they believed that it simply meant that the old-school Tito-restrained former YPA officers who had internalised the Yugo nostalgic -- who had internal analysed the both Yugoslav rather than Serbian loyalty and the particular brand of Titoist communist Yugoslav loyalty as their formative experience in the period of their personal and professional development and that therefore he wasn't someone that they would look upon with approval as the chief of security of what they expected to be a new army for a new Serbian state. Nevertheless --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just so -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. At the same time, they referred with a degree of grudging respect to what I understand was his successful arrest of some Croat demonstrators who were guilty of killing a Macedonian conscript during the demonstrations in Split in May of 199 -- oh dear, it would have been May of 1991. But they specifically referred to the killing of two volunteers belonging to the Serbian radical party in the region of Dubrovnik as the proof that he doesn't like caucades [phoen] Serbian nationalist berges [phoen] and beards, and I now quote from memory. He can't stand caucades and beards, was a comment made at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And who were these individuals again? They were providing security detail for who?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: For the Serbian -- Bosnian Serb delegation. They were -- I have to tell you the truth. I don't remember their names, but they were in their late 20s, perhaps early 30s, and they were the veterans of the early battles. I believe that most of them came from the special police units rather than the military structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned, also, two instances, one with the Macedonian conscript, and then you also mentioned a killing of Serbian radical party volunteer. Do you know if that was the same incident or two separate incidents?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: These would be two separate incidents, and they were referred to with a very different sentiment. The killing of two volunteers was referred to as the proof of Beara's animosity to any display of Serbian particularism within what was still at the time the JNA, but the apprehension of Croat culprits for the killing of the Macedonian conscript was mentioned, as I say, in the spirit of grudging respect as the proof that the man is a pro.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, help me with this: Since you were there and based on your personal observations and experiences, were there any idealogical differences between the civilian authorities, let's call them, in Pale and Banja Luka and those who were former JNA either officers or members; and then if you can, describe that for us.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, even at this distance of more than a decade, it is hard to tell to what extent differences that acquired the guise of ideology were rooted in the differences over personalities, the position in the power structure, or even the accusations of corrupt dealings and outright criminality which was occasionally levelled by the military leaders against the civilian authorities and in particular against the SDS party structure on the grounds. But suffice to say that I became aware of these differences in fairly outspoken references by Dr. Karadzic to the "commie bastards," "komunjare," and the Red Plague, which I do not recall being referenced to any particular person but which I took to imply the top brass, the, basically, top leadership of Bosnian/Serb army. The constant spirit of this underlying animosity was based on the claim that they had divided loyalties and that many of them were still on the payroll of the Yugoslav Army, which at that time was no longer Yugoslav People's Army but was -- became VJ and Milosevic himself, and that they were playing a duplicitous game on the one hand accepting the primacy of the political leadership but on the other still continuing to act as an independent power centre in its own right. On the other hand, the view from the military was that the political leadership displayed a mix of political and diplomatic inaptitude on one hand and the proclivity to corruption and even criminality on the other; that the civilian leadership had failed to proclaim the state of war in the entire territory of the Republika Srpska; that it had failed to control the smuggling of fuel, cigarettes, and even munitions and military hardware, either by the politically connected individuals or through the state company, which even though was supposedly serving the treasury of the Republika Srpska was still in the end allegedly used by the various SDS bigwigs and well connected individuals to line their pockets. But as I mentioned earlier, all of these elements in the puzzle, I haven't been able to glean from any first-hand sources but, rather, from fragmentary accounts and from elements of, you know, press articles and public statements somewhat reinforced by this remarkable level of almost vehement personal animosity that I noticed in Dr. Karadzic on a number of occasions when it came to the top brass of the Bosnian/Serb army collectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And did this attitude, if you will, based on the observations that you've made and had, did this attitude persist throughout the period that you worked as a Balkan affairs analyst, meaning until September of 1995?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: I would say that it was less pronounced in 1994 or maybe early 1995 than it was in the summer of 1995. In the summer of 1995 - that was my final visit - I had two meetings with Dr. Karadzic, one with two Serbian/American people --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And at that time I actually became aware of rather strong language used with reference to the events surrounding the assembly of the Republika Srpska held at Sanski Most in mid-April. Even though reference to what amounted to a coup was not something I heard from Karadzic itself, I cannot exactly recall who made that particular reference or who used that metaphor, but I believe it was an exaggeration that the attempt by the military leaders at that assembly to obtain a number of decisions from the politicians regarding the conduct of the war, the organisation of both the production geared to supplying the military, and the more even burden of the effort on different strata of the population, that was certainly interpreted by the political leaders as an attack on their own position and on -- certainly on their own authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And what time period are you speaking of?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was a two-day assembly of the Republika Srpska. I believe it was April 15th and 16th of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And where was it specifically?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: At Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And who was giving the speeches that led to this, as you put, increased or almost vehement personal animosity that you were generally discussing and this coup that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Obviously I wasn't there, but my understanding is that General Mladic came up with a list of specific demands and that on behalf of the SDS the party secretary Velibor Ostojic responded in vehement terms that those demands were nothing short of an act of disobedience, disloyalty.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And help me with this: Did it ever come other than the conversations you shared with us with the security detail of the political establishment at the Palace of Nations in Geneva, was there any other opportunity that a discussion about Mr. Beara was undertaken in your presence?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: It was either during my January visit of 1995 or my March visit, I can't remember which of the two, that vice-president Nikola Koljevic's Chief of Staff, Zdravko Miovcic, referred to Beara as someone who doesn't trust all these foreign Serbs who have gained access to the political leaders. In addition to myself, he mentioned Jovan Zametica and Milos Prica as, you know, the diaspora Serbs who simply by virtue of living in the West or having lived in the West where one might say suspicious by definition, that therefore, their loyalty was open to doubt, but Miovcic added half-jokingly, but don't worry about it, he doesn't count for much around here, meaning Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just remind us of who Mr. Zametica was at that time?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: He was advisor to Dr. Karadzic. I believe he was particularly focused on foreign and diplomatic affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And the same with Mr. Mitrovic? What was his role?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: No Miovcic. He was vice-president, Koljevic's Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you form an impression as to whether or not they were speaking as a result of their position and their close ties with Mr. Karadzic that perhaps those were his views as well?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Not necessarily, but nevertheless, I found it remarkable that both at the level of, you know, simple but, you know, honest-to-God young fellows who comprised the security detail of the political leaders and at the upper echelon of their entourage, for instance, the Chief of Staff to the vice-president, a fairly similar sentiment was expressed, and also that if what Mr. Miovcic said was true about Beara's dislike of the fact that all these diaspora Serbs are, you know, making themselves conspicuous, that would imply that the security experts in the Bosnian/Serb army took a somewhat dim view of the judgement of political leaders themselves, because if they surround themselves by people who by virtue of having lived abroad are of dubious loyalty, then obviously their own judgements and their own loyalty, perhaps, could be open to some doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trifkovic, the transcript and I misspoke when I used the name Mr. Miovcic, it's M-I-O-V-C-I-C, correct? Is that the way we would spell it?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. It's important just so we have it right. Thank you for that. Now, have you ever heard of Karadzic referred to Beara --

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: -- at any time during any of your visits or the times that you spent in Pale from 1993 to September 1995?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Let me reiterate. The only specific references to Beara by name were the ones made by the security detail at the Palace of Nations in Geneva in late November 1993 and the comment by Mr. Miovcic in either late January or else mid-March of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Share with me, if you will, are you familiar with the name of Bob or Robert Djurdjevic?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was a businessman based in Phoenix, Arizona, who had previously lived in Canada and who was publishing a newsletter called "Truth In Media."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And do you remember seeing him at all in Pale in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember seeing him in a very brief encounter at the office of Dr. Zametica. I don't think it was a particularly friendly encounter because of -- there are two things. One of the two Serbian Americans who came with me on that trip was Mrs. Slavica Ristic from Phoenix, Arizona, who knew Bob Djurdjevic well. They lived in the same city and even volunteered when he started his newsletter with the layout and the data entry but who by that time had come to the conclusion that he was, as she put it, a Milosevic man. That opinion could have been justified some years later when I came across a report in the English language edition of the Haaretz daily newspaper in Israel that in the course of trial of General Sharon's son for corruption, it was mentioned that he received a particular payment from Belgrade, from the government of Serbia and Milosevic for stealing power at that time, which was delivered by Bob Djurdjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Trifkovic, we will go into detail on your visit in Pale, but I just wanted to cover with respect to Bob Djurdjevic whether you knew him or not. Thank you for that. Can you share with us where you were in early -- or in July 1995 prior to you arriving in Pale?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was in Belgrade. I was also briefly in my in-laws' cottage, mountain retreat on Mount Jelica near Cacak, and during my trip to Pale with Mr. Premovic and Mrs. Ristic, I actually left my family in the cottage because having visited Bosnian/Serb republic in the summer of 1993 they were not particularly keen to go, especially since it was the time when military operations were underway. They deemed it wiser not to join me on that trip, and I completely concurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Why did you go?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Because at that time the Srebrenica military operation was in full swing, and I generally wanted to hear what was their take on what looked like an unexpected development. By the way, I had intended to go even before the military operations started unfolding, but when I left, which was July 12th, I was really keen to obtain the kind of firsthand account of what was going on and what was the political leader's take on future course of events so that upon my return to London, which was scheduled for July 18th, 17th or 18th, I could address the media with some degree of authority having been to Pale: Having spoken to the political leaders, having considered the situation with analysts in Belgrade, I can now tell you that this is what's going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And did you provide such interviews or commentary to the news media?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, and one point on which the political leaders were particularly insistent, Karadzic, Koljevic, and their advisors, was that the failure of the United Nations to demilitarise the UN-protected zone of Srebrenica had effectively compromised its status as the protected zone and the military operation was made necessary by the failure of the UN to act in the way that would prevent its further use as an armed camp when raids are carried out against surrounding Serb villages on the one hand and as a UN-protected zone when the Serbs threaten retaliation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, sir, specifically how long you stayed in Pale in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: I stayed -- I stayed from the evening of the 12th until the early morning of the 16th, so I was there the 13th, 14th, and 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And where did you go afterwards on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 16th, I drove to Belgrade, and then either the following day or the one after I flew to London. I really need to look at my old passports to see the stamps in order to ascertain this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to show you what we've identified or are going to use as an exhibit in e-court, which is P2905.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just so the Court's aware, this is an excerpt from an appointment calendar for Radovan Karadzic in July 1995. It was used in the Milosevic trial, and although I understand now we do have what purports to be the complete calendar, this one was used, I think it, as my learned friend has told me, is almost if not identical to the one that was recently seized, but we're using the one given to us by the OTP previously?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just to -- this is obviously an important document. We did not purport we have the complete version of this diary, but we did provide what we do have, that what we know we do have from the recent seizure of that diary, and it matched what came out of the Milosevic trial. So we have -- I think it's roughly the month of July for the diary, but we did have the material that was included that came out in the Milosevic trial, just so that's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just so it's further clear, this is the document from the Milosevic trial. We didn't go through -- since we were only given the seizures from Radovan Karadzic only yesterday, this is the one that was actually used in the Milosevic trial, so...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, both of you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trifkovic, you are looking at, obviously, as you've heard, what purports to be an excerpt from an appointment calendar for Radovan Karadzic for July. Specifically, I think it's the 13th and 14th of July, 1995. Do you see that on your screen?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: There's an English version to the left, and do you have both versions there?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, except that I don't see the bottom of the handwritten Serbians. Oh, there we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you see your name depicted anywhere on that entry after the 13th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Both the 13th with the two visitors from the US and on the 14th with Dr. Zametica.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's take it one step at a time if you don't mind. The entry which is at the top portion of this exhibit P2905, the 13th of July, how many times is your name entered there? Do you see?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Just once under the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And what time does it designate?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: There seems to be some hash marks or minus signs or plus signs to the left of the names of some of the purported visitors with Dr. Karadzic. Can you explain that to us?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know for fact, but it stands to reason that when appointments are made a minus sign would be put next to the name, and if the appointment is actually realized, then the cross or plus sign would be completed. But if for whatever reason the appointment was not, then -- or if it was rescheduled, then the minus would stay because the third from top on July 14th Professor Karadzic and V, presumably Velibor Ostojic, we have the minus sign and -- with the addition tomorrow. So I would say that wherever you see the plus sign, that meeting had actually taken place.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And so what does it say with respect to you in the meeting that you had with Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: For the 13th. We're only talking about the 13th.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. Originally, I seem to remember that we were supposed to have at least a brief meeting with Dr. Karadzic on the evening of the 12th because as I mentioned earlier, for the two visitors from the United States it was a matter of something -- they wanted purely formal and ceremonial reasons and especially as people who had also provided a lot of humanitarian assistance and so on, but we were not able to do so when we arrived on the evening of the 12th. So on the 13th, we had a meeting during which Dr. Karadzic greeted and took pictures and then gave a rather optimistic account of the likelihood for the, you know, speedy political and diplomatic conclusion to the war because with the fall of the eastern enclaves, we are probably going to enter the period of intense diplomatic activity which, as he believed, would pave the way for, you know, a peace on terms favourable to the Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, do you recall who was maintaining the appointment book for Dr. Karadzic in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: There was a secretary. I believe her name was Mira. I really can't remember her last name. I may have been told it at some stage, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just so we have a better understanding of the entries there, to the right of the name in parentheses, do you know what that -- those designations are?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I would say that once the meeting is completed, she was probably entering the actual times when it was held.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And help us with your meeting and entry on the 13th of July, 1995. How long did that meeting last, first to the best of your recollection, and then we'll compare to the entry.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't have been able to tell you from my recollection what was the duration. I would have said more than an hour, less than two, and this sounds about right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Does it just give the length of the meeting, or does it designate the time that perhaps the people met with Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: I would say that this actually indicates the time when visitors came and left.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And what does it say for your entry on the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is that the only entry that bears your name on the 13th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the 13th, it is the only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let's move, then, on to the 14th of July. Do you see any entries that bear your name?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I do, but can you bring the handwritten page down? Yes. We are -- there we are, second from bottom. Myself and Zametica, meaning Dr. Jovan Zametica, 2305 until 0035 -- 25 to 1 a.m..

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, looking at this document, do you -- and we mentioned Mr. Djordjevic. Do you see whether he met with Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We see his name entered from 5 p.m. until quarter past 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's far for me. Does it say actually 5 p.m., or does it have the military --

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Actually, it has 1700. All designations are military style.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me take you to the next document, and we'll come back to this in short order, and I'd like you to now look at 2D531. And it's a long document, but I'd like first for Mr. Trifkovic to see the front page of it so he can become familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speakers are kindly asked to slow down and to pause between answer and question. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry. I will bear it in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trifkovic, this 2D531 exhibit is something the Prosecution provided us during this case, and it seems to be a diary of sorts from Bob Djurdjevic as indicated on the first page, and I think -- from my understanding its his handwriting on the bottom right-hand corner where he says not to open until after the YU war ends -- after three years after the YU war ends. I want to go to a couple of entries in his diary just to see whether it matches or not with the appointment book that we were just looking at. So I would ask with respect to this diary that we go to immediately to - and I think I have the right number here - 2D40-0508.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you contesting this?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's a doc ID --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because we could skip this if the Prosecution does not contest the -- what would be the outcome of this piece of part of the evidence? We can skip it if it's just for confirmation of what is contained in the diary and the appointment book.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's not just that. It also goes to the authenticity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, okay, then -- but the way you described that was as if it was just that. Okay. Go ahead. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I was getting there, though. It's more than a...

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you see the entry before you, sir, that from this diary of Mr. Djurdjevic that he says that he had a meeting with Radovan Karadzic and the time that he notes that he had this meeting in Pale?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it would seem to fit the entry in the appointments book.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, if we just go a couple of pages prior to that which is Doc ID number 2D40-0504, which is the date that Bob Djurdjevic writes as the when the meeting took place. And as you know, we looked at the diary from the 14th when that meeting took place from 1700 hours on. He in his diary, however, writes that it seems to have taken place on the 13th of July, 1995. I'm not going to ask you if you remember what day that falls on, but I will take you further back to Doc ID number 2D40-0491. If we can just look at that entry. That also is July 13th, 1995, but it's a Thursday, and it's actually the start of Bob Djurdjevic's trip from Belgrade to Han Pijesak with a driver called Milos Tomovic. Now, with respect to the dates is it fair to say, and I know you didn't read the entire article, that the meeting that Bob Djurdjevic had, as did you, with Radovan Karadzic actually occurred on the 14th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: I would say that we had two meetings. One was with the visitors from the United States on the 13th, and the other was with Dr. Zametica in attendance late at night on the 14th. I'm sorry, Mr. Ostojic. Are you referring to my own meetings?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I wasn't, and that's what I was looking at.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's okay. I'm just looking to get some help to see the authenticity of this document. Now, the 13th of July, 1995, we see from Bob Djurdjevic's diary that he actually arrives in Pale on the 13th, and he has no reference to meetings with Dr. Karadzic, but his only reference is the next day, which he state is th 13th, which is an error, at least according to the appointment book, correct?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. The 14th was Friday, not the 13th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I object, obviously, to the form of question. It's leading, and he suggested the answer to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It had been better had you stood up earlier. It's over. So let's -- but in future try to avoid leading questions, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I will. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, do you -- I'm going to show you an entry that Mr. Djurdjevic makes -- strike that. Let's go back to the appointment calendar of P2905. I want you to walk us through some of this, and thank you for your assistance on this, and once we get it up we'll be able to look at it, I guess. I want to in particular focus on the 14th of July, 1995, and the meetings that Dr. Karadzic seems to have had on that day. But first I want to ask you this question: Do you know a person or did you know a person by the name of Miroslav Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't recall ever hearing his name or meeting him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And can you share with us, please, whether you can identify his name as having purportedly had a meeting with Dr. Karadzic on the 14th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, indeed. He figures on the list at 1100, 11 a.m., as scheduled but actually held from 1240 until 1310. Sorry. Yes. It is somewhat unclear. It looks like Deronjic himself had a meeting, 1240 to 1310, and then with the delegation from Srebrenica later that afternoon from 1425 until 1825. This is potentially somewhat confusing, but I presume that this is what it means because in the handwritten notes it looks like the meeting was scheduled for 1100, that's the figure on the left; that it was actually held between 1240 and 1310, that's the numbers in parentheses above his last -- his first name; and then the subsequent meeting with the delegation, since it is right next to his name, presumably he was with that delegation from 1425 until 1825.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm sorry. I object to this line of questioning. It's clear that this witness doesn't have any personal familiarity with this book. The book speaks for itself. Everyone can read what it says, and this line of questioning is completely inappropriate to pursue with this witness because all we're getting from him is speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you wish to comment, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think we can determine as to whether or not the book has any level of accuracy and authenticity because this witness was a participant in several meetings, and he can confirm whether or not approximately he met with Dr. Karadzic at that time. I think it's likewise very important for this Court to know when Miroslav Deronjic met with Karadzic at least according to the appointment book. It is indeed relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What you haven't answered is the following: There is the document itself, which purports to say that, but is the witness in the position to confirm that indeed a meeting took place between Deronjic and Karadzic on that day at a time or at any other time?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: By him describing his meeting and the hash marks --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He can only confirm -- he can only confirm that he himself had this meeting, but can he confirm -- yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we have a brief discussion without the presence of the witness. This, again, is an important document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. The witness needs to leave the courtroom because the discussion will be in English, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, who wishes to go first?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I apologise for interrupting Mr. Vanderpuye on this, but this, again, goes back to -- perhaps folks don't know, but Mr. Karadzic's secretary was interviewed about these pages and described what these marks meant, and those statements are available. I believe they've been provided to people, and we can sort this out through that so it's clear to everyone. My memory is I think his speculations are correct, but I would stand by Mr. Vanderpuye's objection that these are about the numbers and who's meeting with who. Those are speculations. However, you know, whether he saw Deronjic, whether -- you know, those sorts of things are perfectly appropriate. But I am sure -- we can go over those -- the secretarial interviews with Mr. Ostojic and get this sorted out. I don't think it's, frankly, a big issue, but it can be sorted out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment. I'll give you the floor, Mr. Ostojic, soon. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We support Mr. Ostojic's position in relation to this, Your Honour. In this diary, it's clear that Bob Djurdjevic spoke at some point to this witness. That's detailed in the diary. And in our submission, it's perfectly permissible to ask the witness about other parts of -- sorry, I'm not going to -- other parts of the diary. Diary is confusing because, of course, we are dealing with Karadzic's diary and Djurdjevic's diary, and I am referring to Djurdjevic's diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but I --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If the objection relates to Karadzic's diary, we take no stance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's how I was understanding it to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's my fault, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's how I was understanding -- if I am wrong, I apologise, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll only enter the fray if it relates to Djurdjevic's diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. I never understood it that way. Otherwise, I wouldn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's my fault. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please not overlap. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I apologise to you. Mr. Ostojic, your question did relate, indeed, to the Karadzic appointment book and not to Djurdjevic's diary?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Specifically, it did, but we were going to go back to Bob Djurdjevic's diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but that's another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay, well, just so the Court knows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think it can be seen from Mr. Vanderpuye's objection that most of this we don't have any problem with, but when he starts speculating about what the secretary's meant is where finally we've said -- you know, Mr. Vanderpuye's objection. And just so people know -- and out of an abundance of caution, can we go into private session for one second?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's go into private session for a short while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can we please have the appointment diary back on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understand it is. The appointment diary, Karadzic appointment diary, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, it is on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, let's look at -- and we'll get back to it on the 13th of July, 1995, in your meeting with Dr. Karadzic. You started to briefly tell us who was in attendance at the meeting, and share with us, if you will, what was discussed during that meeting.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: There wasn't really a discussion. It was more in the form of a fairly long and detailed monologue, I, Dr. Karadzic, on what I remember as a rather optimistic view of developments and his confident expectation that with the fall of the two enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa we are on the threshold of a diplomatic solution to the war by which I believe he implied the realization by the western powers, primarily the United States, that the Serbs had the wherewithal to end the war by military means and that they, meaning the western powers, will finally come up with an offer that was better than, as I remember him putting it, the meaningless offer of the contact group, which consisted of nothing more than an unacceptable map. I wasn't sure at the time, since we didn't have a private meeting, whether this was actually what he believed or whether it was more of a - how shall I say - public gloss for the other two visitors. But in view of the fact that the meeting lasted a fairly long time and that my own views were distinctly more dim regarding the likelihood of a speedy political solution on terms favourable to the Serbian side, I was particularly keen to meet him one more time, which happened the following day in the presence of Dr. Zametica when in fact even, you know, without the presentation of visitors he reiterated what I can only call a rose-tinted view of developments and predictions about the future. So -- unfortunately, my precise notes about the meetings were lost when my computer crashed, and I had not had the copies of the files. That was back in the late '90s, but my overall impression from those meetings was that he was in an upbeat mood and believed that the end of the war was on the horizon in the form of an improved political package that would give the Serb Republic the elements of sovereign statehood within whatever Bosnian package was finally negotiated. As I say, I did not agree with that analysis, but on the basis of previous similar encounters I did not argue the point, either.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, immediately under your name we see a name of another individual. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Vladimir Dimitrijevic. I know that the man. He is a Serbian Swiss publisher.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm looking at the English version. On the 13th of July, 1995, we're still talking about.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's okay. The meeting that you had with Toma and Slavica and Dr. Karadzic, immediately under that entry by your name Dr. Karadzic had another meeting, correct?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't want to get into the interpretation of the diary. I would say that on the basis of what's in parentheses that meeting must have taken place before our meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I could see that, Mr. Trifkovic. I'm not suggesting the meeting, just the name beneath yours.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Tomo Kovac. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Toma Kovac was at that time?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: No. It rings a bell, but I don't have the precise recollection of his function.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, had you met with Dr. Karadzic on the 13th of July, 1995, other than on one -- this occasion and for that approximately one hour and 40 minutes?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What did you do on the 13th of July, 1995, during the day when you didn't have this meeting with him?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: I also had a meeting with Professor Koljevic later that evening, and also during the day, I do not recall exactly at what time, I had a lengthy conversation with Dr. Zametica.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And share with us that meeting you had with Professor Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: It was in the evening hours, and Professor Koljevic was also in an upbeat mood, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Tell us who was present. I'm sorry for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that there were both his Chief of Staff, Zdravko Miovcic, and Karadzic's advisor, Zametica, in attendance.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And you were starting to tell us. What were the discussions to the best of your recollection at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Professor Koljevic shared Karadzic's optimistic predictions and upbeat mood, and he was also planning to go to Srebrenica the following day, as he put it, to provide reassurance to the civilians that they would be treated properly, which, by the way, was a point strongly emphasized by Dr. Karadzic, and I had the distinct impression that at that point Dr. Koljevic was not -- functioned under the impression that the civilians were still there. And obviously, I myself was not in the position to know what was the score on the ground, but in retrospect I found it remarkable that Professor Koljevic on the evening of the 13th seems to have believed that he would be going to -- the following day, the 14th, and that the civilians would still be in Srebrenica. It implied to some extent, again, looking back with hindsight, that maybe the left hand didn't quite know what the right hand was doing over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think it may be time for a break, but we can go on, whatever the Court wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. Shall we have a 25-minute break now? Okay. 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trifkovic, we're going to try to complete this more efficiently if you don't mind. And now, we're looking at the 14th of July, 1995, and can you remember as you sit here whether you had a meeting with Radovan Karadzic on the 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, even without the diary I would have remembered that it was a meeting late in the evening with Dr. Zametica in attendance. It was a fairly short meeting and far from giving me some useful insights that would have been at odds with this upbeat and optimistic assessment given on the 13th in the presence of two visitors. On that occasion, Dr. Karadzic broadly reiterated the points already made this that meeting. In other words, his firm belief that the military successes were heralding the political and diplomatic end game that would work out to the Serbs' favour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And do you recall how long that meeting lasted on the 14th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, having seen the appointment, it would indicate about an hour and a half. I seem to remember -- or rather, my impression from -- or my memory from that meeting would have appeared to be a bit shorter than that. It didn't in my memory feel like an hour and a half, but that's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, let's turn to Mr. Djurdjevic's diary again, and the doc number is 2D40-0507. As that's coming up, do you remember meeting with Bob Djurdjevic on the 14th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: I believe I already mentioned that we had a brief encounter when he entered the office of Dr. Zametica where I was at that time using his computer because he was feeling unwell, and I went to the office to write a letter from Dr. Karadzic to A.M. Rosenthal, the former editor of the New York times, and also to translate a press release into English that he -- no, sorry, Zametica asked me -- he, meaning Zametica, asked me to do on his behalf and pass it on to the SRNA news agency.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And as you're looking at this exhibit, which is a portion of Bob Djurdjevic's diary, he also has your name depicted that he saw you there, on the top of the page, as you see, on 2D40-0507. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And it reflects, also, a meeting or an encounter with him in Jovan Zametica's office?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: I can tell from that brief summary that the mutual love and affection between us was fully reciprocated.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We won't get into the contents of that, but thank you for that. I wanted to ask you, the day of July 14, 1995, did you have any other meetings with Radovan Karadzic other than that which you've testified to?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, let's go to the next day, the 15th of July, 1995. Did you have any meetings with Radovan Karadzic on the 15th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: When was the last time you had any meeting or had contact with Dr. Radovan Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: It was on the evening of the 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And then can you tell us when you departed Pale?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: I departed Pale early in the morning on the 16th. In fact, the 15th I remember taking Mrs. Ristic and Mr. Premovic just for walks around. We may have driven up to Jahorina, and it was not a day filled with substantive meetings, and I don't have much of a memory of that last day. Certainly, it wasn't significant in terms of conversations or encounters.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And sir, have you ever met Ljubisa Beara?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's all the questions I have. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ostojic. Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No question for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Thank you. Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. No questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. No questions. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lazarevic. Madam Fauveau, s'il vous plait?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Merci, madam. Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I have some questions for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Trifkovic. My name is Dragan Krgovic, and I appear on behalf of Milan Gvero. I have some questions for you. Since I'll be asking you in the Serbo-Croatian language, and I can see you've already taken your headset off, I'd kindly ask you to wait until you've completed my question in order to answer so as to avoid any overlap. You said here that on several occasions you went to Republika Srpska and that you met with certain individuals. Did you have occasion to see or meet my client General Gvero?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: I did have two encounters with General Gvero that I can remember, and also I met him once with a group of other people where we didn't have an opportunity to actually talk. The first such occasion that I do remember was in July of 1993; and the second, it was on my way back from Pale at a hotel or restaurant of the hotel at Han Pijesak on the roadside, which would have been either in late January or in late March of 1995 on my way back when I believe that General Tolimir was also in attendance. The first meeting was also my very first visit to the Republika Srpska, and I remember remarking to General Gvero on the need for someone who is fully proficient in English to be appointed their - meaning the VRS, the Bosnian/Serb army - spokesperson, and that ideally it should be a diaspora-born Serb, hyphenated Serb from either the US or Canada because in the western world to a large extent the medium is the message, and if the messenger is fully proficient in the language of the intended target audience, then the message itself will be more readily accepted. As we had seen with the example of the Muslim foreign minister, Sacirbegovic, Sacirbej, as he was called in the English-speaking world, whose fluency in American English was a great boon to their side of the story. I don't recall the exact date of the second meeting, but I know that my overall comment to General Gvero and I believe there were Tolimir and maybe one or two others was that -- and I tried to be as tactful as I could knowing the tensions between the political and the military leaders, that I wanted to indicate that I do not share the optimistic assessment of the political situation that was prevalent at Pale, and I'm now talking about early 1995, the aftermath of Jimmy Carter's visit, and yet another set of assurances from Dr. Karadzic that things were just hunky-dory and that in fact the political and diplomatic solution was going to favour the Serbs and would not take a long time to come. My impression is that on both occasions, General Gvero was just listening to what I had to say rather than engaging in, you know, an active two-way conversation. I certainly had the impression that my point about the need for an effective spokesperson fully bilingual was well taken, and whether it was acted upon, I don't think because we would have known about it. But on the other hand, the fact that he did not actively comment on my somewhat gloomy assessment of the prospects for a negotiated peace favouring the Serb side, which by the way had been a constant theme of my various visits to Pale, that his reluctance to comment upon that may have reflected, you know, the desire not to appear explicit about the differences that must have existed between the military and the civilian leadership on this point just like on many others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Trifkovic, for a very thorough explanation. When answering to my learned friend Mr. Ostojic's questions, you mentioned certain comments made by President Karadzic when he commented on the VRS top brass.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please show 2D531 to the witness next, ERN number 2D40-0510.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trifkovic, it is the third paragraph from the bottom. There's a sentence uttered by Mr. Karadzic talking about General Gvero. [In English] "Mladic and a small number of communist pig." [Interpretation] The part beginning: [In English] "The RK said that judging by the reaction most officers were shocked to learn that. It was clear that the coup was being planed only by Mladic and a small number of communist pigs, 'komunjare,' around him like Gvero. He said Gvero is one piece of human garbage." [Interpretation] Mr. Trifkovic, such expressions, have you ever heard Mr. Karadzic utter those things when talking about the generals of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: I have to admit that the particular term, "djubre coraka," "human garbage," I haven't heard, but I have heard the term "komunjare," which Djurdjevic translates as "communist pigs" and maybe should be more colloquially translated as "commie bastards." I have certainly heard it often enough, and I also seem to remember this "Red Plague" term, although not in particular reference to General Gvero, although from the context of his remarks I think it would not be difficult to guess that he would regard General Gvero as part of this inherited milieu of ex- JNA officers to which whom he - had how to put it tactfully - serious misgivings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know why Karadzic singled out Gvero in that context? Do you know what was General Gvero's role and function in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what was the exact formal title, but I know that he was in charge of relations, public relations and that he had the role of port parole of the Republika Srpska military. I don't know the exact context of the remarks referring to the meeting of May the 1st, but that meeting would have been two weeks after the session of the Republika Srpska assembly at Sanski Most on April 15th or 16th at which, as I know from open sources and my own reading of many years later, General Gvero was present and was at least implicitly one of those supporting the 25 points that represented -- at that time by Mladic that represented as specific demands from the political leadership for the more effective waging of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the result of the work of the assembly was that they made a recommendation for General Gvero to be pensioned off?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of General Gvero being singled out by himself. I believe that shortly before the fall of the Krajina, and now we are entering into an area where I don't have any firsthand experiences or knowledge based on personal encounters, but I believe that it was shortly before the fall of the Krajina in the first week of August that an attempt was made to pension off a whole group of senior officers including not only General Gvero but also General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Trifkovic. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: No questions, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon to you. Good afternoon to my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And good afternoon to you, Dr. Trifkovic. My name is Kweku Vanderpuye. On behalf of the Prosecution, I'm going to put some questions to you in relation to your direct examination and also in relation to your cross-examination. So if there's anything that I ask you that's not clear to you, please let me know and I'll try to rephrase it in a way that we can better understand one another. Now, you mentioned that you never met Colonel Beara.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: I have no recollection of meeting him. I was present on a few occasions in gatherings where several people were present, for instance, in the area of Gorazde when there was a reception. I'm not aware of meeting him, and I certainly have no memory of exchanging any words with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. But you've -- you learned his name, and you heard him spoken about in 1993, you mentioned, right?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The -- I remember him mentioned by name in November of 1993 and then again in early 1995 on the two occasions that I described.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you indicated that you had gone down to Pale from I think it was Belgrade on the 12th of July, 1995, right?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
