utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And about what time did you arrive at Pale?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: It was towards late afternoon, early evening. I would be hard-pressed to give you more precise time than between 530 and 7 or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And for what purpose were you going?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: I was spending the previous ten days in Serbia on -- as part of the summer break and was going to visit, anyway, at some point in order to learn the details of what was going on in the aftermath of the Srebrenica operation which, of course, was very much in the news at that time, although obviously not for the reasons that we are mostly concerned these days. And the two friends of mine from the United States - independently of each other, by the way - were also in Serbia, and it was a sort of friendly favour that I took them along pay a visit which both of them very earnestly wanted to make. But my primary interest was, to put it colloquially, get the score on the what views from Pale were, which I could then usefully employ in my own analysis, writings, and media presentations.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And the two friends you are talking about are Tom Premovic?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And Slavica Ristic?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter 3690 in e-court, please. If we could just go down and blow up, that's probably okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This is another entry from the appointment book of Dr. Karadzic, and with respect to your name, you see it appears on -- below 12 July 1995. It's the second line following the date.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you see below that the name of Vukcic?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you know who that is?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recognise any other names that you see on this particular page, that is, under the 12th July date?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: And by the way, let me add that this meeting was not actually held.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah. We were supposed to arrive somewhat earlier, and the secretary informed me that the meeting was rescheduled for the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And when did you learn that the meeting had been rescheduled for the following day?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Upon arrival at Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you recall the name of the secretary who told you that?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: As I mentioned earlier, I believe her name was Mira, M-I-R-A, but my visits were not frequent enough to establish any kind of rapport with administrative support staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you -- well, following the rescheduling of the meeting, did you meet with anybody else on the 12th?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The transcription says "were not frequent" -- all right. Sorry. On the evening of the 12th, the only -- the only person I recall meeting, or rather, persons were Dr. Koljevic's Chief of Staff Zdravko Miovcic and Dr. Karadzic's advisor Dr. Zametica.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And were these meetings -- were these meetings actually scheduled beforehand or were they scheduled simply after --

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I knew them privately, so to say. I -- they were not people with whom you would need to formerly schedule a meeting. They were people who I actually relied upon to give me informal behind-the-screens briefing of what's going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And with respect to the rescheduling the rescheduling of the meeting that you had for the 12th, were you given an explanation as to why the meeting had been cancelled?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: That our arrival was later than had been anticipated and that, therefore, his schedule for the evening was full.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. When did you make the appointment actually, initially?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: When I called Dr. Zametica to say that we would be coming, and I believe it was only done a day or two before we left Belgrade because I'm pretty certain that I wasn't able to fix the dates until at most two days before leaving.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. The reason, as you can imagine, I'm asking is because there's no time indicated for your planned meeting.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the details are somewhat blurred after all these years, but I believe that I would have been advised to give them a call once I actually arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: And in view of, you know, crossing the border and checkpoints and so on, one couldn't be very precise about the timetables and schedules.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sorry. Can we have the B/C/S version of that appointment calendar moved so we can see the full writing on the right-hand side of that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Vanderpuye speak closer to his microphone or more into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it good enough like that?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If that's the best they can do. I'm just told that in parentheses it has an indication of something, and maybe it might assist us to have the witness inform us what it says.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Or if they have the original, they can share it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it probably means for tomorrow because it says "za se" [phoen] so it would be "za sutra."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you'd mentioned that you'd met -- you'd had some meetings after this particular meeting was cancelled, right? These are private meetings?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: As I say -- I wouldn't necessarily call it a meeting. It was a private conversation that had more of a character of a social get- together with, you know, snacks and drinks and informal off-the-record chat about what's going on, who's doing what to whom, what's the mood, what's -- it would be, as I say, the kind of friendly briefing that you get from people you know personally rather than people who are communicating with you on the basis of their function or the chain of authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And what is the nature of the informal conversations that you had with Mr. Miovcic?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have precise recollection, but I would probably guess that it had to do with the unexpected or seemingly unexpected collapse of the Defence of Srebrenica and the diplomatic implications and what is the take at Pale on the significance of this event and on the presentation of the issue which in -- at that time was primarily focused on -- in my personal interest was also whether there would be the continuation of the military activity in the direction of Gorazde, whether they would try to wrap it up in one swoop, and also, what feedback, if any, were they getting from the UN and from various other international powers that be. But I can't give you more precise answer because I know this would be the kind of conversation I would have with Zametica and Miovcic with whom I had both a better personal rapport than with the officials higher up and also with whom I was able to be more frank about my disagreements or differences of opinion than would have been the case with someone like Karadzic or even Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, seeing as you've discussed this matter with them, did you get the sense with them at any point as to what direction this particular operation was going?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: I had a strong sense both then and the following day that they were generally surprised that Srebrenica fell effectively without a fight and that there was also some difficulty in getting the feedback from the ground as to what was actually going on. I remember while I was with the other two visitors at Karadzic's office the following day that on a couple of occasions he actually was interrupted and tried to get the connection through to someone at Han Pijesak, but one particular term I remember used is that the line is down. So what I got from those two gentlemen was the sense that they really didn't know what happened, that after, you know, a long period of tenacious defence that Srebrenica just fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, did you discuss some of the concerns that would normally arise in the situation like that, such as humanitarian concerns?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. What did you discuss?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: That it would be very important for the Serbian side to make sure that nothing happens in the treatment of the civilians and, by the way, the focus was primarily in our conversations with the civilians that would be used in the way that during the different episodes earlier on with Gorazde, with Bihac, and of course, Sarajevo itself that there was immediate treatment of the Serbian side that was greatly detrimental to the Serbian interests, which was at least to some extent, even though possibly exaggerated, but at least to some extent based on real events. I had the impression that they shared this assessment, and I also have the impression that during the meeting the following day, Dr. Karadzic was particularly insistent that he would issue orders that nothing would happen to the civilians that could be used in the media presentation as a tool against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, why did you -- what gave you the impression that they shared that particular concern?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Because I commented on, first of all, that I saw a number of civilian buses, that as we drove down from the Drina River, from the Serbian border towards Pale, I didn't see much in the way of traffic, military or civilian, but there were certainly buses parked by the roadside especially in the area where the road turns left towards Bratunac from the main highway from Zvornik to Sokolac. And on that first evening, which is the 12th, I have to emphasize that my own knowledge or understanding of what was actually going on was sketchy in the extreme. On the other hand, I again have to reiterate that even the following evening, the 13th, Dr. Koljevic, the vice-president, expressed intention to go and visit Srebrenica the following day, the 14th, which would at least suggest that he, also, was not fully appraised of the fact that the civilians had been removed or were being removed at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. If I could, could I have 65 ter 2047 in e-court, please. 2048, I'm sorry. Page 58 through 61. 58 through 61 in the English. Page 43 in the B/C/S, please. All right. I don't see it yet. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What you have in front of you now, sir, is a -- it's a broadcast of an interview with Dr. Karadzic on 12 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In particular, the reason why I've put it up on the screen for you to see, it relates to the information that Dr. Karadzic had on the 12th of July, and in particular it touches upon some of the concerns that you raised with Mr. Miovcic in your meeting with him as regards the humanitarian concerns following the fall of Srebrenica. If we could -- first of all, have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you can see on this page, that is, ERN 92454, that

utterances.speaker: DR. KARADZIC IS SAYING
utterances.text: "Our army is enabling the establishing of our civil authorities there because the Serbs were exiled from Srebrenica at the beginning of the war." You see that, right?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Further on it says: "And there is now as affairs settle down an activity of the refugees who want to leave." Before I go on, let me ask you first: Did you have any of this information on the 12th pursuant to your meeting with Mr. Zametica and Mr. Miovcic?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did this particular issue come up at all?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: It came in the general sense that it would be important for the Serbian side to avoid any mistreatment or appearance of mistreatment of the Muslims, not only as a matter of principle but also in order to prevent the media treatment of any such incident in the way that would magnify it and render it politically useful to the other side. In other words, it was more a discussion in principle of an issue that was presumably going to be on the agenda in view of the fact that there were large numbers of people in Srebrenica. So it wasn't prompted by any specific information I had. It was simply the discussion that presumably I would have had if at that time either Bihac or Gorazde rather than Srebrenica was on the agenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. So your understanding from your conversations on the 12th which were followed up with Dr. Karadzic in a sense on the 13th was that it was important at least from the point of view of the western press that was there was the appearance that humanitarian treatment of the refugees is being appropriately administered, right?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: No. What I was not saying is that there should be the appearance, but rather that such treatment should be substantively so in order to avoid the media presentation of -- or rather, misrepresentation of the appearance of mistreatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for clarifying that. If we could go to the next page, please. Now, if you go -- sorry, we also have to move forward in the B/C/S. Now, if we could go all the way down to the bottom of the page in the English. All right. I would say about the fifth line or sixth maybe or seventh line from the bottom, you can see it says "secondly". This is in response to a question put to Mr. Karadzic: "Mr. President, what information do you have on the humanitarian situation in this town?" And I'll refer you to where it starts: "Secondly..." It says: "Our commissaria for refugees as you can see rushed in to help. Everyone can see that these people look well-fed and that there are no problems at all. If you compared what happened in western Slavonia where the Croatians were allegedly liberating with what has happened in Srebrenica where the Serbs are doing the liberating, there is such a difference that it is impossible to talk about war at all." Now, first of all, I just want to ask you: Did you discuss western Slavonia at all during your conversations with Mr. Zametica and Mr. Miovcic?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember that I did. I can only tell you if we did what I would have said about western Slavonia. I would have used it as one of the arguments for my constant misgivings or unease that Milosevic had some kind of deal with Tudjman and that the overall lay of the land didn't look right to me. The way that western Slavonia fell, and as indeed it happened with the Krajina on a grander scale in August, reflected my constant suspicion that the powers that be in Belgrade were striking deals that were detrimental to the western Serbs' position.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you discuss with Mr. Karadzic at some point what his consideration or concerns were about western Slavonia as they related to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't have any memory of that. I do remember, however, that in the meeting on the 13th he stressed that the treatment of the Muslim civilians in Srebrenica will be such as to put the Serbian side beyond any reproach even by the non-benevolent media.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And when you say non-benevolent media, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: I would say that he would regard most of the western mainstream media as not friendly to the Serbian side in their reporting or analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And in fact, you yourself have referred to the situation in western Slavonia on a number of occasions in interviews that you gave, right?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: I would need to look at those interviews. It's been a long while, and I believe, yes, that I did make a number of observations about it at the time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Well, in particular -- I don't think we have this in e-court because it was just provided by Defence counsel last night, but let me read it to you, and let me see if that refreshes your recollection. This is an interview with BBC TV Newsnight live. It's dated 28th May, 1995, and it's entitled: "UN Making Mockery Of Its Own Resolutions." Interview with Dr. S. Trifkovic. Presenter: Peter Snow. And in this interview, the question is put to you: "What is going on? Have the Serbs now thrown all restraint to the wind?" In your answer. You say: "If mockery is made of UN-protected zones, it is of the UN's own making. They are not enforcing their own resolutions when it is the Croats and the Muslims who are violating them. The Serbs are fed up. They are feeling very irritated because only three weeks ago in western Slavonia we had a slaughter of Serb civilians. We had a mass exodus of Serb civilians, and the UN did nothing. They did not even castigate the Croatians in the security counsel; ditto with the misuse of the safe havens." Is that essentially what Dr. Karadzic is referring to in this 12 July broadcast interview?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, let me emphasize that I did not either receive inputs from Pale or seek them in my presentation of -- in fact, the mood of the Serbs at that time was more than amply supplied by the media from Serbia Proper or Republika Srpska. It was the early days of the internet, but it was already possible at that time to have it at one's fingertips, if you will, not video streaming but certainly written reports. And my judgement on what happened in western Slavonia in the first week of May of 1995 did not need to rely on Dr. Karadzic's assessment. If the two coincide, it is probably because there was some substance to such an impression, that, indeed, it was an attack in violation of the UN rules, and that, indeed, it was both brutal and indiscriminate when it came to the treatment of the Serb civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Well, I want to talk about your independence as a -- I've forgotten the term that my colleague used but what I understand it to be is an unofficial spokesperson for VRS, but we'll talk about that separately. But let me equate you with a different news article, if I could, and this is one from London news radio, and this one is dated Monday, 17 July 1995. I don't think I gave you the time for the last one, but I have the time for this one, and that's 2135. And it's entitled: "Consequences Of Failure To Demilitarise. Live interview with Srdja Trifkovic. Presenter: Paul Reynolds." And the question that he puts to you, he says -- well, you finish the previous paragraph saying: "These places have not been demilitarised." He says: "But is that an excuse to have the Muslims of Srebrenica ethnically cleansed?" And in your response, you say: "In the Balkans, one ethnic group does not trust soldiers belonging to another ethnic group. In the hundreds of years of civil and religious wars in the Balkans, this has been a regular feature. Only two months ago we had a tragedy on a much greater scale in western Slavonia, also nominally a UN-protected area, where the Croat army attacked the Serbs, drove them out, and massacred hundreds of them. There are 600.000 Serb refugees in both Serbia and the Serb republics of Krajina and Bosnia." Okay. Now, this is a separate interview, obviously, and it's dated just about a week -- well, five days after the interview with president Karadzic. Now, in relation to your statement there, were those statements predicated upon your conversations with Dr. Karadzic or your understanding of what Dr. Karadzic is referring to on the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in fact, no. If you read my response to that particular question, I'm actually making a factual statement that is amply supported by the empirical evidence of the wars of Yugoslav succession, that, indeed, the ethnic group that is faced with the sudden change of authority in a given territory will do its best to depart the territory because it does not trust, and I'm not either quantifying the degree of unpleasantness of one group towards the other or trying to qualify in any way that the Serbs behaved necessarily better or worse than the other two sides. I'm simply stating a fact that has been a regular feature of warfare in that part of the world for a very long time, that if, for instance, the Croat troops come into the area of Neretva valley, the Serbs from Mostar will run away to Trebinje or Nevesinje, or when the Muslims overrun parts of central Bosnia, the Croats will be the ones who sometimes even using Serbian territory will escape to Croatia proper, and needless to say that the Muslims when the Serbian army advances will feel more comfortable going to Tuzla or Zenica than staying put. It is, I would say, more of a descriptive factual statement than analytical let alone value judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is the 65 ter number, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Judge Kwon, this doesn't have a 65 ter number as yet because these were provided to me last night by Defence counsel. So I'm only -- I'm not tendering the documents as it were, per se. I'm only putting the questions to the witness, and if it becomes an issue then I think I'll have to pursue the course to enter the documents into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Kwon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. In fact, in the interview that Dr. Karadzic gave on 12 July 1995, he says -- oh, it's only -- okay. Page 60 the English, and that was 65 ter 2048. Let me just read it in the interim so that we can move along. He says -- all right. It's there now. It's the third line from the bottom on this screen. It's page 45 in the B/C/S, I understand. "I would also like to remind the entire international community of a particular hypocrisy. Whenever Muslim forces from these safe havens advance through the Serb territory from Bihac" -- as you've just mentioned -- "Tuzla, Sarajevo" -- as you also mentioned -- "and even from Gorazde, the whole word applauds. But when the Serbs undertake counteroffensives and neutralise their opponents, then the world starts to wail and mourn Over the losses. You can see that the Muslim civilians haven't lost anything, but the Muslim army has." Now, did you have any information as concerns the Muslim civilians when you spoke to Mr. Miovcic and Mr. Zametica on the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Other than the agreement with the absolute necessity of acting in the way that would be beyond reproach and other than the indication given by Koljevic that he still believed that basically they were there on the evening of the 13th, no. However, I was becoming aware that the evacuation was underway or had already taken place at the tail end of my stay, ironically more through listening to the BBC World Service than being told firsthand by anyone over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I could have 2748, please, in e-court. All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This is an urgent combat report. It's directed to the president of the Republika Srpska, and it's dated 12 July 1995. Let me ask you this: Have you ever seen a document like this before?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: No, and in fact, this would be the kind of documents that I normally wouldn't see or, indeed, expect to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. If I could go to page 3 in the English. It's the last bottom of paragraph A. 6(a), I'm sorry, and I believe it's page 3 in B/C/S. At the bottom of this paragraph, that is, where it says under number 6, "In the DK zone of responsibility," Drina Corps zone of responsibility. Paragraph A, "The enemy..." At the bottom of that paragraph, you'll see it says: "The enemy has been attempting to withdraw from the Srebrenica enclave with women and children in the direction of Ravno Buljine and Konjevic Polje but ran into a mine field." Go to the next page, and we look at B, "Situation In The Corps." And I think it's the next page -- it's not. Okay. It's in the middle of the paragraph in the B/C/S. At the bottom of that paragraph, that is paragraph 6(b), it says: "On..." and then slashes, "... important axes, parts of our units in the MUP have laid ambushes in order to destroy Muslim extremists who have not surrendered and who are attempting to break out of the enclave in the direction of Tuzla." So my question to you is in respect of the information that is contained in this report, did you have any discussions on the 12th, or for that matter, on the 13th as regards these Muslim extremists who have not surrendered and are attempting to break out of the enclave?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: In order to answer this adequately, I have to emphasize that on the 12th I drove with two visitors from Zvornik from Karakaj border crossing to Pale on that very road, and at the checkpoint outside Zvornik driving south we were warned of the possibility of small armed groups crossing the road and that we were proceeding on our own responsibility. We were not either told to take a detour or advised not to proceed. We were also told that in case of any such movement, it is better -- best to avoid contact or to make a U-turn, but certainly didn't look like they were overtly concerned at the level of military activity was such that it would make the trip risky. So I have to admit that on the basis of what looked like a fairly uneventful drive through the very area that -- of Konjevic Polje and the vicinity of Bratunac and Tomorici and from there up to Vlasenici and so on that I already arrived at Pale, maybe lulled into a false sense that the military activity was practically over.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: But I was certainly not aware of -- in fact, the conversations at Pale proceeded with the assumption that it's over, the enclave has fallen. There was, you know -- I believe you know, imminent expectation of the news of Zepa, but I wasn't aware at that time of any attempts by the armed groups of a significant size and magnitude to break through.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. So nobody at Pale when you had these conversations within the circle of the Presidency actually discussed this particular information with you --

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- at least not on that day?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: The focus of the conversation both on the first day when I came with the two visitors from the United States and on the second day late in the evening when I was there accompanied by Dr. Zametica was on Dr. Karadzic's view of the political diplomatic aftermath of Srebrenica's fall. In other words, on the first day I heard what looked like, in my opinion, excessively optimistic assessment, and on the second I really hoped to have a more realistic conversation, but having encountered even, you know, in -- in a more -- without the presence of the first-time visitors, having encountered a similar outlook, I basically did not argue the case because on a number of previous occasions, assessments that I regarded as faulty or poorly based by Dr. Karadzic, I tried to enter into some kind of analysis in terms of real politik and scenario-making, and I never got very far with it. On the contrary, I could sense that the discussions based on the non-acceptance of favourable assessments were not welcome or encouraged.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with respect to the information that you received concerning these small armed groups, did you receive that before you crossed at Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, no, but I think that it stood to reason to assume that in such immediate aftermath of what at that time one assumed was a fairly major military operation that it would be necessary to obtain the information from the military on the ground about the possibility of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: And that's why I mentioned this relaxed attitude of the Serbian soldiers at the checkpoint exiting Zvornik because I didn't have any specific information about the level of military activity, but I assumed that it was possible that some was still in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: But in fact, somebody did tell you that you should be aware of --

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- small arms groups?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was the soldiers manning the checkpoint exiting Zvornik in the direction of Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. So these are VRS soldiers, right?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And they had the information concerning these potential extremists that are mentioned in this combat report?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in retrospect I would say that their demeanour was more relaxed and --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, they're further away, too, right?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: But I would say that, you know, in retrospect and with hindsight I would not have made that drive. It was maybe their assessment or their impression of the situation but certainly that we were told that, yeah, we should exercise caution, but it was not presented in terms of, you know, serious warning that there is some likelihood of encounters that could be dangerous.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I think I may have forgotten to ask you, but you tell me if I've repeated the question. I'm sure my colleague will tell me. When you met with Mr. Zametica and Miovcic, did you meet with them alone, or did you meet them, also, with Mr. Premovic and Mrs. Ristic?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that Mrs. Ristic was tired and was not with us. Mr. Premovic would have been with us at least part of the time, but it was -- I really can't be sure. But the conversation was certainly of the kind that had more to do with background briefing of the overall mood of the place rather than end, you know, outlook, hopes, expectations, rather than any specific information that would preclude the desirability of a third-party presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Did you meet with anybody else following your meeting with Mr. Zametica and Mr. Miovcic --

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm pretty certain --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- on the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, I believe that was it. In fact, it was getting on, anyway, and it had been a long day.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Now, you've indicated that you also met -- you met with Mr. Karadzic on the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: That was with the visitors from the States, yes. It was on the 13th in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And this is when you described his upbeat monologue that he delivered?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you indicated, also, in relation to your contact with Mr. Karadzic that you had some notes concerning these conversations that you had between -- well, over the 13th and the 14th, right?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think I had my laptop with me on that particular occasion, but I would have entered then from scribblings, brief notes made at the end of the day. However, with my laptop crashing I believe in 1997 and the backup diskettes not covering some of these -- in fact, it's a source of great regret to me personally. But to be perfectly frank, I had the overall sense of deep frustration and misgivings, not for the first time, after what was yet another encounter with the inability of Dr. Karadzic to look at the predicament of the Republika Srpska in the full complexity of the wider international situation, and I make no qualms about that. I think that that meeting would have been yet another occasion for such sense of frustration that the view from Pale was rather narrow and based on wishful thinking rather than a comprehensive analysis of the global diplomatic and political situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Now, you mentioned that you met with Mr. Karadzic on the 13th for between one and two hours.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: I believe from the diary it would appear that it was about an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you met with him in the company of Mr. Premovic, Ms. Ristic, right?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Was anybody else present during the course of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Zametica came in and out but was not present throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And during the course of your meeting with Dr. Karadzic, was he in contact with anybody else, any soldiers or --

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I remember him shouting a few times, give me connection, what's up with the connection, "veze su u prekidu," who exactly he was trying to contact, but I also got the sense that some lines were down.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. How did you get that sense? Did somebody say that specifically?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: He actually said something like [B/C/S spoken] or something like that. Whether it referred to the film connection or some other form of communication, I'm not sure, but I believe he was actually shouting this to the secretary, so it must have been the film.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. But -- okay. How many times did he shout this during this hour and a half that you were with him?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: I would say two or three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And did he have access to any other telephones that were there?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Occasionally, the phone would ring, and -- I wouldn't be able to say how many times, but yes, our meeting was being interrupted, and it wasn't a particularly structured meeting in that it was mostly his resume of how he saw things to the visitors.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. You said that he seemed -- well, "buoyant" is, I think, too strong a term, but optimistic?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Upbeat, optimistic. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And was that because he felt as though -- well, tell us why that was, what your understanding was of that.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: This would really take us into the overall propensity of Dr. Karadzic to look upon the situation of the Republika Srpska in a more optimistic and more upbeat manner than was warranted by circumstances or by the attitudes of the great powers. For instance, the hope or expectation, even, that Russia would take a more strongly pro-Serbian position had been a salient feature of his comments and remarks throughout the -- I wouldn't say each and every time I came, but I would say that the majority of times he would say something like, "Rusija se budi," "Rusija progledava," Russia is waking up, Russia is coming to see the light, an opinion I didn't share. I actually believed, and as we know in retrospect, this is correct, that Yeltsin's Russia did not want to confront the West over the Balkans at that time. Likewise, I think that his hope or expectation that some kind of diplomatic deal or offer was imminent is another salient feature of his comments in the winter of 1995 January after the visit of President Carter or, for that matter, in the spring of 1994 after the Gorazde operation. So all the time I had the increasing sense of frustration with the inability to communicate my understanding of the problem of the Bosnian/Serb position as seen from the other side of the Atlantic or from London in the way that would be readily understood because ultimately I realized that in a very deep cultural sense we did not speak the same language.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, speaking of language, what exactly did he say to you during the course of this meeting? What exactly did he say in terms of his position concerning the operation?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Because of my lack of precise notes, I can only give you the best recollection I have of the meeting after 13 years, which is that he was greatly optimistic that the outside world will realise from the success of Serbian arms in Srebrenica that it is futile to expect the Serbs to continue taking punishment and not getting the elements of a political package that it can live with, and he expressed repeatedly his confidence that in the near future as the result of this demonstration of Serbian military might, there should be a political movement and diplomatic movement that would actually wrap up the war. I do remember -- and I'm sorry, before coming here I didn't call Mrs. Ristic or Mr. Premovic to compare not notes but memories, but I do remember his saying that the war is coming to a close. Now, with hindsight we know it was but certainly not on the terms he had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I think this is probably a -- am I wrong about the break time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We still have another 15 minutes for the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Very well, then. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: However, that said, if you prefer to have it now, we can have it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now would be a good time, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Right, we'll have a 25-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could I ask you, how much longer do you think you require?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think about -- well, half an hour, 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And do you envisage --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Not much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Then think about who is coming tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We'll talk about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Trifkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could some microphones be turned off, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I was asking -- I'm sorry, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. Just checking to accommodate the interpreters. Is there anybody else with his microphone or her microphone on apart from me, which I will switch off immediately now. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Trifkovic, when we left off I was asking you about your meeting with Dr. Karadzic on the 13th of July, and I'd asked you specifically what he had said regarding the operation in Srebrenica. Can you tell us what, if anything, else he said during the course of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of my conversation with Dr. Zametica and Mr. Miovcic the previous evening, I recall being curious about the military details of what seemed to be rather sudden, unexpected, and swift fall of Srebrenica on which he didn't really enlighten me. In fact, to be perfectly honest I left Pale and the Republika Srpska on the 16th still none the wiser as to what actually happened in terms of the military aspect of the operation itself. Bearing in mind the tenacious fighting in Bihac in the fall of 1994 or Gorazde in the spring of 1994 or Srebrenica in 1993, I have to admit that the issue as to what actually happened to make the fall of this enclave so swift and so unexpected, at least my impression was that to them up in Pale it was unexpected, that I still didn't get the answers to that particular question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, I understand that, Mr. Trifkovic, and I appreciate your response. But my question to you is specifically what it is that Dr. Karadzic told you during the course of that meeting, and you understand the distinction --

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- between that and what your impressions of what he said are?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: I have to confine myself to overall impressions because I don't have the minutes, and after all this time the memories tend to acquire the character of overall impressions rather than specific snippets or quotes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I understand that, too, but as you recall, you did testify about a conversation that you had which concerns Mr. Beara in 1993. I take it you don't have notes of that conversation?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, no, but it was, nevertheless, to someone who had encountered these grassroots soldiers from the ranks, if you will, for the first time. It was a memorable experience because it was also the first time that I sensed first-hand this latent mistrust bordering even on animosity between the two traditions among the Bosnian Serbs. It would be a characateur to describe as the partisan tradition versus the Chetnik tradition, but it was certainly something of that spirit at work there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Trifkovic, at that period of time in particular, that is, on the 13th of July, 1995, you were still functioning in some respects in the capacity of dealing with the western media regarding specifically the information that you came to acquire?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, when it comes to the attitude of the western media to the issue of Srebrenica, I became aware of the question of what happened to the military man or man of military age only after returning to London. In fact, the theme of conversations that I had was solely the treatment of civilians. The issue of the treatment of military prisoners didn't even come up. But again, to give you a very precise answer, I didn't find that particular visit useful when it came to articulating positions in media interviews. I didn't find the optimistic scenario for the future useful. I certainly wouldn't have condoned it or shared its overall tone.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, maybe I've misunderstood what you've said, but on your direct examination I believe you said that you came down -- the reason why you went to Pale was to get information about the specific goings on as concerns the Srebrenica operation for the purpose of dealing with the western press or the outside media. So my question to you is this.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If that's the reason why you went there and you actually had an appointment and spoke to the object, the purpose of your being there, you spoke to the president of the Republika Srpska, and he spoke to you about the specific incident that you were there to inquire about, but is it your testimony that you have no recollection of what he told you on the 13th of July knowing --

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- knowing now in retrospect what transpired on the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: No. My answer is that it wasn't particularly fruitful or useful meeting from the point of view of having either a closer understanding of what was going on on the ground or of getting an insight into the political background and the realistic scenario for the end game from which Srebrenica might lead. So whereas it is, indeed, very much the purpose of my visit to have a clear picture, from the meetings with Dr. Karadzic far from getting clear picture, I get an upbeat story of the war entering its finale on terms favourable to the Serbs and the absence of clear description, even, of what actually happened to make Srebrenica fall quickly and unexpectedly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you ask the question?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you ask him what happened to the military that was in Srebrenica --

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, actually, the --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- that is, the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: The issue of what happened to the military had never arisen until that moment, and I'll tell you why.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I just want to know if you asked.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: It didn't occur to me because in all previous operations the prisoners -- my understanding was that the prisoners were regarded as valuable assets to be exchanged for one's own side, and I had no reason to believe that this was an issue, and I didn't ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I take it you asked about civilians?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Very much so because --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I expressed the opinion that I already shared with Miovcic and Zametica on the first evening, that it would be extremely important to avoid any incidents or exercise that would be detrimental to what I believed was very sensitive political situation of the Serbs at that moment and that Dr. Karadzic gave me assurances on this point. In fact, I believe that I was also given a press release in Serbian about these assurances to translate into English in the absence of Dr. Zametica for further distribution by the SRNA news agency.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what did this press release say?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: If there is a record of the SRNA news agency releases for that period, you might see the precise wording, but my memory is that it contained specific guarantees that their safety would be -- that they would be looked after and they have nothing to fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Now, I've asked you a lot of questions and a lot of time as concerns about -- as concerns what Dr. Karadzic told you on the 13th. Is it your testimony that you have no specific recollection as to what he spoke to you about or what he said, I should say, over that hour and a half to two hours that you were with him on the 13th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, it wasn't two. It was an hour and a half during which time some interruptions due to phone calls and his attempts to make them were taking place. Some of the time was taken up by social niceties connected with the introduction of the two visitors, but I am being perfectly frank with you when I say that what I recall of that meeting is, first of all, a very long discourse on the end game which he confidently expected to follow that would be favourable to the Serbian point of view; and secondly, the agreement with my insistence that it is both substantially and in terms of media relations extremely important to avoid any incidents in the treatment of the civilian population that would be reminiscent of the early stages of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And that's your best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: It is, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that you had you notes concerning these meetings that you had with Dr. Karadzic on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Particularly what I recall, and I don't know if the record of it exists somewhere else, was a letter that I wrote to A.M. Rosenthal, the former editor of the New York Times, by Dr. Karadzic in which he praised his editorial published a few days previously and made some specific suggestions about the renewal of direct contacts between the Clinton administration and the Republika Srpska leadership. So this is the closest I can get to some specifics of our conversation that were contingent upon his overall favourable assessment of the situation, that he felt so confident that in fact the situation is ripe for some kind of diplomatic end game that he approached Rosenthal with a suggestion that such -- that he explores the possibility of such contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The notes that you referred to that were on your computer, you say they were destroyed?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: No, they were not destroyed. I had what they call a hard disk crash --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: -- either in late 1996 or early 1997, and I had not been doing backups in a timely manner at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, what did you do about it? Did you try to get your hard drive fixed?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, but it was -- I was not able to recover anything, which in fact is a source of great anguish to me personally, not that it matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I can imagine. Do you have that computer?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: No. It's been discarded.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It's been discarded?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Many years ago, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you keep any handwritten notes?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, no, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Forget the computer because the computer you will discard, for sure. It's the hard disk itself. Did you keep the hard disk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, no, because it would have meant dismantling it. Once I was told by the Best Buy technician that it was a matter of a basically catastrophic failure, the business of defragmentation - and I don't know the technical jargon - was, as I again recall, beyond their ability to take care of but might have been done at a considerable expense by some expert company specializing in that kind of problem, which I in hindsight regretfully decided not to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sorry, you say that computer crashed in 1996?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: In the winter of --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. So you had it for a good year after the events in --

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: It was a brand new computer that I took with me to Serbia, but I didn't take it with me to Pale. It was actually the first colour laptop that I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you produce any articles based on the information that you had in that computer, the notes that you took?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, no, because I must emphasize, the meeting with Dr. Karadzic was both disappointing in terms of his analysis and not particularly informative in terms of the background to the specific military circumstances surrounding the fall of Srebrenica. So on the basis of that particular meeting, I did not write anything or publish anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. But you did have contact with the press after that, right?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, and in fact I don't think that my comments to the press would have been much different if I had not gone to Pale at all in July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In other words, they were not specific, but they were general comments that you made?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Even if they refer to -- again, you have some advantage over me because I haven't actually been revisiting my old interviews in awhile. But suffice to say that the only point that I came with was the assurance that the civilians would be treated well, and also, let me add the reiteration of the insistence that military operation was necessitated by the failure of the UN to demilitarise the enclave. But there was nothing new about that. That had been the old theme early on in the spring of 1994 in connection with Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Trifkovic, you met again with Dr. Karadzic on the 14th -- well, first, before I get to that, I'm sorry. On the 13th -- and you'll correct me if I'm wrong, but I think you mentioned on the 13th that he had mentioned something about Zepa?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was taken more or less for granted. I have no recollection whether Zepa had already fallen or was about to, but it was pretty much taken for granted that it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, let me ask, again, then: What did he say in respect of Zepa on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Again, I can only say that he said with Srebrenica and Zepa, we have proven that the strength of our weaponry, our military prowess is such that it can no longer be assumed that the Serbs will accept any terms of final settlement that do not address their key interest. I don't know even on what specific day Zepa fell, but I think with that he assumed that it was going to happen as a matter of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. You met with him on the 14th, right?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 14th. It was quite late at night. It was with Jovan Zametica, and the specific purpose of that meeting as far as I was concerned was to try and see if there was a more nuanced and a more critical view or understanding of the overall political and diplomatic situation than the one displayed the previous afternoon. In other words, to be perfectly frank, whether he was playing to the gallery with Serbian/American visitors who are prominent in their local community and presenting the upbeat front for their benefit or whether it was indeed what he believed, and it was indeed what he believed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, since you recall so specifically what he believed, can you recall what he told you on the 14th?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that it is possible to recall the overall tone, flavour, and "stimmung" is the German word, which maybe the best in English equivalent would be -- yeah, the overall tone is good enough, without recalling the specific quotes. He was saying that the war is coming to a close, that the Serbian military success in Srebrenica will present the world with the reality that can no longer be denied, and that after this we can look forward to the diplomatic movement which will finally be based upon the realisation that the Serbs cannot be defeated and that they will not accept a settlement that does not address their key concerns. Yeah, I'm again quoting from memory of many years ago, but again, what I found remarkable is that in a more private meeting, in a different setting, just with his advisor Dr. Zametica in attendance, he essentially repeated the same-old, same-old, which I found deeply flawed both in terms of the rigor of analysis and in terms of the understanding of the diplomatic facts of life.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well -- and forgive me for this, but I'm a bit puzzled. You're a historian by profession, by training, right?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You have a PhD --

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- in history?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: An historian is a kind person who remembers dates, events, places and things of that nature very well, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can recall them?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: I would argue that, in fact, it is far more important in the study of history to remember the essential underlying intent of the key participants rather than their verbatim quotes. We don't know exactly word for word who said what to whom in July 1914, but we do know that the underlying tendency was for Wilhelm in Germany to give Austria a blank cheque to deal with Serbia as she deemed fit. And if you ask me how --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Trifkovic, you are were in the middle an historic event concerning the former Yugoslavia, full-out war, and you were there in the midst of it with a note pad, with a computer, and for the specific purpose of gaining access to information that would help you discharge your obligations to the -- to the civilian authorities of the Republika Srpska. That's why you're there, and you're a historian, and you're telling this Court today that you have no recollection, specific recollection of what Dr. Karadzic told you on two separate occasions on the 13th and 14th of July, 1995, knowing fully well looking back what was occurring on those days? You know that on the 13th of July, 1995, that people were being killed?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: I know now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know then.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, you knew that in 1996.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: I have to remind you that I've tried to give a fairly detailed and comprehensive answer about the essentials of that conversation, and my inability to reproduce -- and my inability to reproduce verbatim quotes is really based on my respect for occasion that we need to get -- to understand the character of that meeting rather than try to and reproduce unreliably the specific, quote-unquote verbatim segments of it, and in that respect I've done my best today.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I appreciate your concern for the integrity of these proceedings and your respect for the Court as concerns the information that you're providing and the accuracy that you wish to provide it in. Now, you have written a number of articles in the past, right?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you've also testified at these -- at this particular Tribunal in the past as well, right?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: As an expert witness in the Stakic case five and a half years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, do you recall writing an article in 1996 -- a 1996 article called "The Hague Tribunal: Bad Justice and Worse Politics"?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Indeed, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And it is true that you wrote in that article that: "The tradition, that is to say the International Court of Justice tradition which is now being destroyed by a pseudolegal imposter, the Yugoslav war crimes Tribunal, which was inserted deliberately into The Hague to provide the pretender with a legal and cultural pedigree and at that same time devalue the true legacy."

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: "It's as if Jimmy Swaggart set up shop in Rome, took a crash course in Latin, and took to wearing a miter." Did you write that?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You also wrote that: "This so-called Tribunal uses legal language. It has jurists on its panels, and they are dressed in a bizarre imitation of continental judicial attire." And you said that "It has funds, lots of funds, but it's a fraud." Right?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: It's been a few years, but certainly, the sentiment is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Well, in fact, what you said on page 13790 of that transcript, that is, in the Stakic case, is that -- yeah, that's a verbatim section of the article published in June 1996, and you readily admit that you have considerably modified your views of the Tribunal since then. That was back in 2003.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Right. That's what I said, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in fact, other than the comments about the judicial attire, you still hold the view that the Tribunal is in fact a fraud, don't you?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: I would say that this has to be somewhat qualified in -- on several counts. First of all, I think that the Tribunal is an extremely important forum for the presentation of the historical record. Secondly, I believe that some of the decisions of the Tribunal, particularly in the Haradinaj case and in the Oric case would only reinforce skepticism of its modus operandi and its process, but at the same time that because of the need to set the historical record straight as comprehensively and as dispassionately as possible, I certainly respect it as the forum in which the attempt to get a very complex story analysed in as comprehensive a manner as possible is indeed here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Well, you wrote -- I should say you said, rather, in an interview with BBC, and this is 65 ter 3684. I don't think I enter it into e-court. You'll let me know if you want to see it. All right. You were asked this question, and this concerns -- well, let me give you the date first.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: 22nd of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: 22nd of July, 2008, and you were asked about the indictment of Mr. Karadzic, and you were asked specifically, "Do you think the war crimes were committed?" And your answer to that was: "The war crimes were committed. Absolutely. What remains to be seen is to what extent the war crimes committed by the Serbs will continue to be treated as uniquely more substantial, more evil, and more massive than those committed by the other two sides." Do you recall giving that answer to that question?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you stand by it, don't you?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Because you think -- well, in your opinion, I should say, this Tribunal is anti-Serb?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: No. If you look at that quote, I said it remains to be seen. Which means I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So you're optimistic?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm still giving this Tribunal the benefit of the doubt that after two verdicts that, indeed, would reinforce the skepticism about its nature and its underlying premises, the Haradinaj and Oric case, we may as yet with the Karadzic case get a more dispassionate and more evenhanded treatment than the one that, as I say, we've seen in those cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: It would sound haughty and arrogant for me to say that I'm giving the Court the benefit of the doubt, but hopes springs eternal.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, do you think that that somehow makes it sound less haughty or arrogant?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: No, it is maybe a human touch that the lawyers will take as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You have expressed the view that you expect Mr. Karadzic to be convicted because the verdict has already been written, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the verdict I didn't say was written by the Court, but the verdict but the media chorus and of the commentators on each and every flickering screen and printed page in the world is not only written; it's cast in stone.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And that's your view as you sit here testifying before this Tribunal today, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You've also written several pieces with respect to your views about Muslims, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: We have to draw the distinction between pieces about the Muslims and pieces about the Islamic ideology. I would appreciate if you'd let me know which of the two you particularly refer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, I'm referring to Muslims. Let me refer you to 65 ter 3687. This is an article that you wrote. It appears to be on the 24th of November, 2003, and it's entitled: "Islam and Slavery: The Concealed Truth. Excerpt from a lecture by Srdja Trifkovic." Xavier University of Louisiana, New Orleans, 14th -- I'm sorry. This is 14th November, 2003.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I don't know if we can go to page 6 on this one. I'm on page 6, and I guess we'll get there. You see the paragraph which begins: "It is richly ironic", right?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What it says below that is it says: "The violent and inherently discriminatory message of the Koran is a huge problem for all Muslims. We cannot solve it for them, and we should not be asked to deem the problem solved by pretending that the Koran is a pacifist tract." Right?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And that's your view with respect to not only Islam but as to all Muslims, right?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I don't see where you see the connection.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I see the connection where you say "all Muslims."

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: It is the problem for all Muslims, and some Muslims resolve it by choosing to reinterpret the Koran while others stick to the view that the Koran is the unadulterated view of Allah, which is immutable for all time and cannot be interpreted but must be taken literally. And there is a great deal of distinction between saying that it is a problem for all Muslims and further saying, which I'm not, that all Muslims regard the Koran as literal -- in its literalist way, the way that, for instance, the Muhabis do and the way that in which the Rema [phoen] of the chief centres of learning ital alaskar [phoen] university do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, let's look a little bit further down on the page if we could. Looks like it's just about the last sentence on that paragraph, you say: "The West has yet to learn fully the lesson that my Balkan ancestors were forced to learn six centuries ago, that Islam a collective psychosis seeking to become global, and any attempt to compromise with madness is to become part of the madness oneself." You wrote those words, right?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You believe that Islam is a collective psychosis, right?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do, but without putting it in the context of the literalistic interpretation, it wasn't conveyed. In other words, you are taking this totally out of context.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Am I?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: If we say that in the discriminatory message of the Koran is a huge problem and if we, then, say that Islam is a collective psychosis without reference to the particular problem that the Koran presents with its inherently discriminatory message, then it would be necessary to explain whether this collective psychosis reference refers to each and every Muslim believer or to those who take the Koranic message in its literalist sense. This is where I think you have to look at it in the totality of my piece and not in isolation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Well, looking at it in that context, then, it would make sense that people that are not Muslim should seek ways to defend themselves, right, by disengaging from the world of Islam physically and figuratively?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: That --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Does that make sense to you?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: That disengagement is indeed something that I have long advocated, which is vastly different from attempts to intervene in the Muslim world and to "bring democracy to the Muslim world." In fact, I think that from the civilisational point of view it is far more productive, far more promising of a peaceful discourse to disengage than to engage in the way that engagement has been practiced in Mesopotamia and Afghanistan.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. So that means it would make sense to separate from somebody from the Islamic faith, right? Because that would be the most practical solution to the problems that you've identified in Islam, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: It would indeed be the best advisible strategy for the western world to deal with the problem of Jihad, not by trying to bring counter-Jihad to the heartlands of Islam but to, indeed, disengage in the way that would preclude open-ended military commitments that are only helping the Jihadists obtain new recruits for their cause.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. In your article dated January 26, 2007, this is called Dines Vedemi [phoen], and that was published in Chronicles Magazine, you say -- 65 ter 3693 for the record. "It's never happened before because" -- well, let me go back so I can put this in context. "Now, think how amazing this is. Has it ever happened in this country - I'm not talking about some totalitarian country, but America - has it ever happened that a prominent intellectual called on leading writers on a subject of major importance to stop writing what they are writing because it would offend someone?" That's your question. You answer it. "No, this is has never happened before. It has never happened before because it is only in response to Mohammedinism that westerners adopt the posture of preemptive surrender which Batjar calls mental dhimmitude. Of all the social, ethnic, religious, political movements in the world, only Islam has the ability to evoke this eagerly cringing attitude. Only Islam has this faculty of inducing people to surrender" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We need to look at the original of the text on the screen in order to be able to interpret it correctly into B/C/S. Thank you. Because we don't see it on the transcript, either, because it too fast. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. If we could go -- it's on the second page -- or third page of this document, and reading from paragraph 8, it's the third paragraph in that series. I'll start here where it says -- it's the third line from bottom of the page on the screen: "Of all the social, ethnic, religious, political movements in the world, only Islam has the ability to evoke this eagerly cringing attitude. Only Islam has the faculty of inducing people to surrender psychologically to it even before it has any actual power over them." You believe that, right?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in fact, this is -- that's yours, quote, but I agree with it, that in fact the self-censorship that the elite class of the western world exercises when it comes to misogyny, violence, and the active attempt to change the liberal nature of the western society in order to accommodate the views and beliefs that are not shared by the overwhelming majority of the host population is, indeed, unprecedented. I think that the level of self-censorship witnessed in connection with Muhamed's cartoons, for instance, or with the non-reporting of the dark side of family violence among the Muslim diaspora in western Europe and so on reflects this fundamental truth, that if there is any other social, ethnic, religious, or political movement that is guilty of such transgressions, for instance, deep southern evangelical Christianists, or in terms of ideologies, members of either far left or far right movements, the level of public indignation of the media class and of disclosure and unmasking of the facts of the case would be far greater. I think that it is not even particularly unique nowadays to complain of this tendency to self-censorship. You will find it in articles by Stein or by Robert Spencer, by -- in fact, it is beginning to come from both the left and the right, that one does not help either the continuation of the liberal character of the western society or the integration of the Islamic community to gloss over the unpleasantness that is all too often present. And yet, the media editors prefer not to dwell on it because not only is it tricky; it can be physically dangerous as unfortunately Vince - I said almost Vincent van Gogh - the documentaries van Gogh found to his peril on the streets of Amsterdam not a million miles from here a few years back.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In your article, this one's dated 27th February, 2002. It's called: "Islamic Terrorism In Italy: The shape Of Things To Come" by you. That's 65 ter 3688. If we could go to the bottom of the page. Oh, wait a minute. If we could go to page 3, please.
