utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President. If we could just go to page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we could -- all right. You see this paragraph that leads "Britain leads the way"?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, in the paragraph you mention in the second sentence of the second paragraph below it where it says "Islamic law" --

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- in brackets. It says: "In Britain today where Islam controls the inner cities..." Now, I'll grant you this article was written in 2002. Now, when you make this reference to inner cities and Islam controlling inner cities, do you have any particular cities in mind?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is actually something that needs qualification. The inner cities does not refer to areas not inhabited by Muslims, but on the other hand, there are significant areas of some inner cities, specifically Leeds, Bradford, Birmingham, Leicester, parts of east London, parts of other industrial cities in the midlands, such as lower Hampton and also in Yorkshire that, indeed, exist de facto communities under their own Islamic-based rule. You will not find alcohol in any of the shops, you will not find video stores that would offer material not to the liking of the adherence of Mohammed's faith, and you will find that there is a great deal of pressure on local people to conform to such an extent that even young Britons of Pakistani origin are very keen to leave such areas if they do not subscribe to the cultural assumptions and the lifestyle prevalent in them. Again, to those of us who know circumstances in Britain, this I think is neither particularly new nor, indeed, remarkable.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Trifkovic, with all due respect, that's known in some circles as commercialism. One does not sell what another will not buy, and that's why you don't find these things in certain shops in all kinds of places around the world.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: At the same time, those who would try to test the market for alternative products which are not offered would soon find his shop window smashed and his physical security jeopardised, and that is --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And that's what we call the mafia, and that exists all over the world, too, Mr. Trifkovic.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: No, not if it is not motivated by commercial interest but by idealogical convictions of the perpetrators, which by the way is similar to what is it happening in France where young girls who in similar suburbs of eastern valieus [phoen] of Paris do not wear the head scarf, risk getting something called the "smile," which is a knife slash that goes from the angle of the lip to the lower earlobe. So no, it is not the Mafia; it is fanaticism.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me ask you this question. If we could go to page 5. You see that paragraph that leads "Meanwhile across the channel..."

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You write in this paragraph: "In Germany, the highest Court in the land ruled in January 2002 that Muslim butchers should be allowed to slaughter animals according to Islamic practice by slitting their throats and letting them bleed to death and without stunning them first in any way. German law says animals cannot be slaughtered without first being stunned, but the constitutional court has now overturned it. The head of Germany's Islamic counsel Hassan Hosjogan [phoen] declared that this will be an important step in the integration of Muslims in Germany." You then write: "If and when the constitutional court allows a clitoridectomy for Germany's Muslim girls, presumably another important step will be made, but that integration will be complete only when Pakistanis in Britain, Algerians in France, and Turks in Germany turn the host country into an Islamic society by compelling it to adapt to their way of life." You wrote that, right?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you believe it?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Believe what specifically?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, you believe that the only way that a Muslim person can integrate into a Christian society is by turning the Christian society into one that is based on Islamic law, right?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not saying it is the Islamic activists that are saying it, that the only end product of their activism is the complete triumph of Dar al-Islam over Dar al-Harb and if you doubt that this is indeed the self-proclaimed objective of each and every Islamic activist in the world, given the sufficient time I would be more than happy to supply you with ample quotes that settle the matter beyond any doubt. This is not suggesting that all Pakistanis in Britain, Algerians in France, and Turks in Germany are sharing such views. In fact, specifically for the Turks in Germany I would say it is, indeed, a minority. But I'm suggesting and I still stand behind this view that making legal exceptions and exemptions for a religious group in order to accommodate its particular demands only feeds appetites for further demands which are ultimately unlimited in scope and nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much for that, Mr. Trifkovic. I do appreciate your candor.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I have no questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye. Mr. Ostojic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I do not, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That's -- do you have any questions? Do you have? Mr. Trifkovic, that means that we have come to the end of your testimony. I was wrong in the beginning when I imagined you will be with us again tomorrow, but I'm sure you are happier. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, I wish to thank you for having come over, and on behalf of everyone present here I also wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We've sent the list around, but I think it is just 2D531 that we'll be requesting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: There's no objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection from the other Defence teams? None? So admitted. Mr. Krgovic, you didn't use any documents so as of course...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Same documents, so...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but apart from that, in other words, you haven't used anything else. Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just bear with me for one second. I'm sorry. I'm just going through the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We tender 65 ter 3678 through -- 3678 through 3690, and then 3693.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We have to take a closer -- thank you. I'm not sure that -- you know, if they want to bring in the articles, I don't have an objection to that if that's their point, but I don't know with respect to 3690 through 3693. I do have an objection to 3691 and 3692. I guess 3693 -- you're not offering that? I have to maybe have a clarification. Through 3690 and then 3693, no objection, Your Honour. I read it now. I have no objection. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thought you were misreading it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So those documents are also admitted. Now, before we adjourn, what is the position about tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We -- Professor Wagenaar, obviously we haven't been in contact with him since his testimony. He was instructed to be here on Monday. With the scheduling, we really don't have any witnesses in town to present to the Court, and I apologise for that. We just envisioned that -- as I tried to suggest on Wednesday, I believe, that we may have a gap and maybe we should start Professor Wagenaar on Friday because I envisioned possibly a shortened Mr. Trifkovic or an overlapping one. We do not have any witnesses here in The Hague to present for the Court tomorrow, so I do apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was expecting to hear something different. I mentioned specifically before the last break what's going to happen tomorrow in the hope that you will take the hint and during the break try to contact Professor Wagenaar.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I took the Court's hint, and my intern who we gave the two days off because we're scheduled to meet on Sunday morning to prepare, we're trying to get a hold of her and have someone from the victim and witness unit call Professor Wagenaar. We haven't been able to accomplish that. We just can't get ahold of him, nor did we -- I personally didn't try to call him, but we have called our intern who was here, and I know we have scheduled for her to meet with me Sunday morning to go over the transcript and the testimony. That was yesterday when we finished with him. So we can continue to try this evening, and I can get back to the Court on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, of course, everyone else, all your colleagues, Prosecution, forget ourselves because we will be here in any case, but everyone else will have to come here and wait to see what's going to happen in the morning, whether we are sitting or not sitting. This is what I purposely tried to avoid. Yes, one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And in particular, Madam Registrar is also drawing our attention to the accused because to come here they have to wake up early.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I suggested I think on Wednesday that Professor Wagenaar does continue to testify on Friday, and with all due respect to you, I think you mentioned at least two separate occasions and specifically to the witness that he recommence on Monday, and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's because you told me that you required the full day for Trifkovic and another full day was required by the Prosecution, and then Mr. Zivanovic wanted one hour which was -- or 45 minutes which then reduced to 10 and which resulted into nothing today. We can't go on like this. One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope we've made ourselves pretty well understood. Last thing we want to do is to complicate matters, and at least this Trial Chamber as composed tries to be as pragmatic as possible. In our mind, we have got two concerns, that this kind of occurrence should be avoided. The second concern is the Nikolic Defence team, that by Monday first thing in the morning need to know exactly from you, Mr. Ostojic, when you will definitely be concluding your case so that they can start theirs. So what we are going to do, we are going to adjourn until Monday when Professor Wagenaar will continue his evidence. I don't want to keep everyone else hanging until tomorrow morning, come over here, and then go back; the accused wake up at 7 and are brought here only to be taken back after I don't know how many hours waiting for transport. It's simply not done. It's an inconvenience, which should be avoided at all costs. So we'll reconvene Monday morning, no -- Monday morning, Monday the 8th at 9 o'clock with Professor Wagenaar, and you need to tell us Monday morning before we start with his testimony all your definitive plans indicating the day of completion of your case, when you will rest your case.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And we will do that, and we will send out a schedule as we do on Thursdays, which I think we already did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. That, we have received.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: My only troubling fact is I don't know how to rely on the estimates by the other parties and the Prosecution to give you a definitive. I think we can reasonably conclude on Thursday of next week. At the outset, I believe we will conclude by Friday. The only concern is that DutchBat individual who I'm in conversation with my learned friends to see if we can resolve that. Our case wouldn't technically close because we have two witnesses that will b e coming during the case of the Miletic case just so that the Court is aware of it. But I think by Friday we will have -- our case should close with the exception of the DutchBat individual and obviously the two witnesses we've previously provided notice to the Court and our learned friends who are calling on direct as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 8th day of September 2008, at 9 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.59 p.m.,
